articles.text: The replacement of the artificial turf at Becker Field at Havens Elementary School has been delayed and is now expected to be completed on July 22, one week later than initially estimated. The removal of the artificial turf, now 12 years old, began on June 22, and the field currently sits waiting for the crew from FieldTurf to continue the installation. “The FieldTurf crew was delayed, so the turf install won’t start until the middle or end of [this] week,” said Pete Palmer, Piedmont School District Director of Facilities. Signs have been posted at the field announcing the new timetable. The replacement turf will cost the district nearly $300,000. Palmer has actively been looking at ways to reduce the cost by having PUSD staff perform some of the work. During the delay the school staff replaced the rotting perimeter nailer board with composite material, saving roughly $35,000. The original field was installed in 2010 and had a 6-8 year life expectancy. The field was named for Piedmont resident Mark Becker who designed the current Havens School. The expected life span of the new turf is 8-10 years. FieldTurf, the company that installed Witter Field and Beach Field, is providing the materials and doing the installation. The new surface is called “Vertex Prime Turf” with a natural cork and sand infill. This version of the turf is marketed as having a “grass-like ball roll” and “superior aesthetic appearance,” according to Field Turf. The Havens Parents Club raised nearly 10% of the cost to replace the field. Donors that contributed over $1,000 were given the opportunity to have their names “creatively displayed” around the field. The installation of new artificial turf at Becker Field at Havens School has been delayed one week. The expected completion date is July 22.

articles.text: This year the fifth Piedmont Chamber Music Festival will be held at Piedmont Center for the Arts from July 15-24. This festival, while similar to the Menlo Chamber Music Festival and several in Europe, is unique in the East Bay. A highly selective process brings eight of the country’s finest musicians to PCA for 10 days of intense rehearsals and three public concerts. Over a year’s worth of planning goes into each festival. Musicians are hosted for the week by Piedmont families and make life-long friendships with their homestay families. It is 10 days of intense work occupying musicians from morning through the evening. Both the performers lounge and what is now labeled flex space are used for breaks and meals and a place to leave music cases, change for concerts, and meetings. The Festival is the brainchild of 2001 PHS grad Wayne Lee and his wife Julia Han who met while studying and teaching at Julliard, and Gray Cathrall. The original sponsors were the PCA and the Post, but the needs soon required more than just what our capacities could contribute. Fortunately, Piedmonters Susan Chamberlin and John Chalik assembled an excellent team that works throughout the year to make this event a reality. PCMF is now a 501c3 with Wayne and Juliana continuing to provide the artistic vision. We have requested that activity and sound in the building during the festival be kept very low so as to enable this truly wonderful event to again enhance our community’s offering to the area and our own city. All music festivals require significant funding and sponsorships. Tickets always sell out, so we encourage you get yours early. articles.text: Where to get booster shots in Alameda County The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) released information and data on the newest COVID variant, BA.5, on July 8. The Omicron variant has been classified into the following sublineages, according to the CDPH: BA.1, BA.1.1, BA.2, BA.3, BA.4, and BA.5. As of July 6, according to statewide-collected data, 20% of COVID cases can be linked to the newest variant BA.5. All nine Bay Area counties are back on the Center for Disease Control (CDC)’s high-risk category for community transmission as of Tuesday, July 12. State health officials explained that variants and sublineages of variants are to be expected with the COVID virus. “Viruses change through mutations that create new strains of virus over time. This is a normal process that happens with most viruses. We call these strains variants. Some variants rise and then disappear. Other variants become common. Most variants do not have a meaningful impact,” said CDPH Public Information Officer Robert Barsanti. Still, CDPH noted that BA.4 and BA.5 “can partially evade immunity from vaccination or previous infection,” meaning those who are vaccinated or have already tested positive for COVID may get infected. COVID cases were highest in Alameda County this summer the week of June 7. Hospitalizations and positive cases have dropped since then, but remain steady in July, with a seven-day positivity average of 760. “Alameda County continues to experience high COVID-19 case rates as people increasingly resume pre-pandemic activities,” said Alameda County Health Officer Nicholas Moss. “Hospitalizations are elevated at levels like what we have seen since midJune but remain below what we have seen in previous waves, and ICU burden remains low.” CDC expands booster eligibility The CDC has strengthened its recommendation that those 12 and older who are immunocompromised, and those 50 and older should receive a second booster dose at least four months after their first. Everyone six months and older is eligible for a COVID vaccine. “Vaccination with a primary series among this age group has lagged behind other age groups leaving them vulnerable to serious illness,” said CDC Director Dr. Rochelle P. Walensky. “With over 18 million doses administered in this age group, we know that these vaccines are safe, and we must continue to increase the number of children who are protected. I encourage parents to keep their children up to date with CDC’s COVID-19 vaccine recommendations.” You can make an appointment for a booster for yourself or a child at www.myturn.ca.gov, or by calling Alameda County at 510-208-4829 to find a location nearest you. “Do you have any of those good old junk bonds lying around??

articles.text: Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill 54, the Plastic Pollution Producer Responsibility Act, on June 30. It is widely regarded as the strongest plastic reduction policy in the nation, requiring a 25% reduction of single-use plastic packaging and foodware items within the next 10 years. The bill was favored 66-1 in the State Assembly. Senator Ben Allen, the bill’s primary sponsor, said the bill’s passing exhibits “a meaningful, strong compromise that will put California at the forefront of addressing a major global problem.” Heal the Bay, a nonprofit organization that encourages volunteers to help keep California beaches and waterways clean of debris, praised the bill’s passing. “Reducing single-use plastics through comprehensive statewide policy is a priority for Heal the Bay,” said organization President and CEO Tracy Quinn. “During our beach cleanups, 80% of the millions of trash that volunteers pick up is made from single use plastics. [The organization] envisions a solution that moves us entirely away from single-use materials, especially plastics, and focuses on rescue and refill instead.” If single-use packaging is still being produced in California by 2032, they will need to be “truly” recyclable or compostable, according to the bill. Lake Merritt Institute in Oakland is a nonprofit organization with over 100 volunteers whose mission is to clean Lake Merritt of debris and pollution. Since the organization’s founding in 1996, volunteers have removed up to 6,000 pounds of trash from the lake each month. In 2021, volunteers collected 63,690 gallons of trash. Lake Merritt Institute Executive Director James Robinson said that volunteers encounter many forms of ‘trash’ in the lake - including soccer balls, toys, and Lake Merritt Institute volunteers clean the lake of debris, most of which is single-use plastics. even garden gnomes. “[Our cleanup volunteers] focus on the trash that has washed into the lake from the rain,” Robinson said. “We focus on manmade trash, like plastic bottles, bags, styrofoam peanuts, cigarette butts, etcetera.” Lake Merritt Institute has collected thousands of plastic bags and wrappers, hundreds of bottles and cans, and “uncountable” pieces of styrofoam. Beyond the lagoons of East Bay, the bill promises to also ease pollution that plagues ocean-life. The Plastic Pollution Producer Responsibility Act drew high praise from the Monterey Bay Aquarium, which works closely with organizations like Ocean Conservancy, Oceana, and The Nature Conservancy. “California has always been a leader in protecting our environment and health. Now we are setting the precedent for reducing single-use plastic, which harms ocean wildlife and pollutes our communities. I commend the entire legislature and in particular, Senator Ben Allen, Assemblywoman Luz Rivas, legislative staff, and everyone from the many organizations that worked countless hours to craft and pass this first-in-the-nation legislation,” said Julie Packard, Monterey Bay Aquarium Executive Director. “California’s leadership will, once again, set the bar for other states and even the federal government in addressing plastic pollution.” business hours.

articles.text: Pull out your roller blades and other old activities to share with your kids. Recently, I found myself on a Friday evening Rollerblading in circles around a rink to the tunes of a fantastic DJ. Earlier that same day, I was on the tennis court enjoying smashing some backhands. And the day before, I was beading a fun new necklace while my daughter created a bracelet. None of these activities particularly stand out amongst the various things that I do to keep my body moving and creativity flowing in the summer, except for the fact that it has been 20 years since I participated in any of them. I picked up these activities again because my kids are now old enough to be enjoying them as well, so why not? What a great opportunity to engage in play: both my own and with my kids. When I talk with other parents, I often hear about all the reasons we don’t participate in activities with our kids. We don’t have time, we aren’t in the same shape we used to be, fear of being judged for being “too old,” not having the energy to keep up with our kids (or the memory of our younger selves), not prioritizing our creative selves. But part of embracing the fun of being a parent is the excuse to rediscover these kinds of activities that we once loved and that we put on hold because of the obligations of adulthood, parenthood and those challenging early years with pregnancy, babies and toddlers. On my first day on the tennis court, there was a lot of negative self-talk in my head. I had to actively notice the judgmental voice and then tell it to sit down on the side of the court and be quiet. That kind of negativity was not welcome here. I was playing tennis for fun, and once I re-focused my energy just on enjoyment, it turned into a fantastic afternoon. Kids’ language of connection is through play and as adults, we often ignore play. We bypass it for mastery of a skill or we deem it “not a practical use or time.” But sitting on the sidelines, scrolling through our phones while our kids recreate is not going to deepen our family bonds. Yes, our kids are having fun, but are we? Beading is neither safe nor fun with a toddler in the house, but now that my youngest is six and loves to wear all kinds of jewelry, it seemed natural and enjoyable to teach her how to find a combo of beads that she found pleasing and string them to make her own wearable art. And I got to do the same. It is something I used to enjoy, but let it sit on a shelf, quite literally for 15+ years. Ask yourself: • What activities brought you joy as a teenager or in your 20s? • What aspect of that activity could your children engage with now? Note: It does not have to be the WHOLE thing, just a part is a great starting point. • How can I restart this activity in a way that feels kind to myself and safe? • What will I do if the negative self-talk jumps into my head because my ability level is different than it was PK (prekids)? • When can I start? Put it on your calendar and jump into the fun! Nina Meehan is CEO of Bay Area Children’s Theatre. articles.text: Jody Weverka retired from Piedmont High School’s English Department and as the yearbook advisor after 19 years, and a 36-year career which began at age 24 in 1986. Weverka attended high school in Hayward, before attending UC Santa Barbara where she met her future husband Phil. She earned her Master’s degree and teaching credential at Stanford and then took her first teaching job at Monte Vista High School in Danville. She then taught at San Ramon Valley High for 16 years before coming to Piedmont. At Piedmont she primarily taught American Literature to juniors. When asked how her job remained fresh over the 36 years of teaching, she said, “I promise, to the last week I was learning, it was never the same. The world gives you so much curriculum. There’s plenty going on to continuously have a fresh lens on American Literature.” “This is all I’ve done in my adult life, and was what I wanted to do. I think I’ve always loved the power of story; it’s the way people make meaning of their lives and think about other experiences in the world,” said Weverka. Weverka poured herself into her class, from start to finish, sometimes working 70-hour weeks. As the advisor to the yearbook class from 2011-2020 she found an additional dimension to her career in education, beyond academics. articles.text: Walk for Wellness, Piedmont School District’s Wellness Center’s largest annual fundraiser, will take place August 21 through 27 this year. The event is a series of walks around town open to all. The event focuses on physical, mental and emotional wellness. The Wellness Center provides confidential, free on-campus and online counseling to all Piedmont High School, Millennium High School and Piedmont Middle School students. The Center also helps students manage common emotional and social challenges of middle and high school including but not limited to stress, depression, grief, family or friendship conflicts, and substance use concerns. According to Wellness Center staff, approximately one third of high school and one quarter of middle school students receive counseling at the Wellness Center each year. articles.text: Jasper Schuetz, who will be a freshman at Piedmont High this fall, has big plans as a member of the school’s Mountain Bike team. On June 4, Schuetz competed in the Lost and Found Gravel Festival in Downieville, a grueling 60-mile event which he won at the junior level with a time of 5:08:07.1. Schuetz, who was 111th overall out of 337 riders, beat his competitor by 27 minutes. Riding elevation is no easy task. His route started at 4,829 feet in Portola, and ascending to 6,673 feet. “I split it into three different climbs,” he explained. “There was one climb that started at 4,900 feet and ended at about 6,500 feet, and that was the starting climb, which was probably the hardest part of the race. The way I really approached this long race was keeping my head in it and staying comfortable with the pace I was doing. I didn’t want to blow myself out in the middle of the race. The first idea was surviving and then winning,” said Schuetz. To prepare for racing at high elevation, Schuetz camped the night to get his body acclimated to the thin air and made sure to start strong on the initial climb. “I camped the night before to get acclimated to the elevation. At the start, I really just warmed my body up to it. Because it was such a tough climb at the start, I wanted to start with a high cadence and get the lactic acid out of my muscles, and really just clear my body before going up the hill. That ended up working, I rode at a comfortable pace most of the time,” said Schuetz. Prior to the race he trained with Piedmont Mt. Bike Team, the high school team. “To prepare for this race, I was practicing with the mountain bike high school team. I was an 8th Jasper Schuetz describes his preparation and mindset for the grueling 60-mile event at high elevation. grader last school year and I got the privilege to train with the high school team. We would do spin classes, strength and conditioning, rides around Joaquin Miller, and I would compete for the middle school. I was doing some training on my own after the season ended,” explained Schuetz. Another caveat in long races is making sure your hydration and conditioning is on point in order to avoid cramps. Schuetz explains that he trained his body to have water-tolerance in order to go long distances without needing an exorbitant amount of hydration. “I trained for water-tolerance. I would do long rides and not bring water; that sounds like a bad idea, but I was training myself to just be tolerant and limit my intake of water,” said Schuetz. The Lost & Found Gravel Festival event was a combination of gravel, dirt roads, and paved surfaces. Schuetz elected to ride a mountain bike to take advantage of the off-road and mountainous terrain but admits that he lost some time to those on faster pace road bikes once the course hit the flat and paved portions. “The course was a little bit of road at the start and at the end, but it was mostly dirt fire roads. I used a mountain bike even though it was a gravel race and a lot of riders had gravel bikes. On June 4, Schuetz competed in the Lost and Found Gravel Festival in Downieville, a grueling 60-mile event which he won at the junior level with a time of 5:08:07.1. Schuetz, who was 111th overall out of 337 riders, beat his competitor by 27 minutes. Riding elevation is no easy task. His route started at 4,829 feet in Portola, and ascending to 6,673 feet. “I split it into three different climbs,” he explained. “There was one climb that started at 4,900 feet and ended at about 6,500 feet, and that was the starting climb, which was probably the hardest part of the race. The way I really approached this long race was keeping my head in it and staying comfortable with the pace I was doing. I didn’t want to blow myself out in the middle of the race. The first idea was surviving and then winning,” said Schuetz. To prepare for racing at high elevation, Schuetz camped the night to get his body acclimated to the thin air and made sure to start strong on the initial climb. “I camped the night before to get acclimated to the elevation. At the start, I really just warmed my body up to it. Because it was such a tough climb at the start, I wanted to start with a high cadence and get the lactic acid out of my muscles, and really just clear my body before going up the hill. That ended up working, I rode at a comfortable pace most of the time,” said Schuetz. Prior to the race he trained with Piedmont Mt. pages.text: Wednesday, July 13, 2022 13 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 15th year in the Post. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. RAFAELLA GOMES Fencing Piedmont High Class of 2021 UC San Diego Class of 2025 Rafaella Gomes, PHS Class of 2021, is a fencer competing with UC San Diego and the Brazil National Team. In last week’s Post, we covered Gomes placing 16th of 44 in the 2022 Pan American Fencing Championships’ Foil Women’s Senior Individual bracket in Asunción, Paraguay. She also helped Brazil finish fourth among 10 teams. She was the youngest competitor on the Brazilian team. In the 2021 Junior South American Championships, Gomes won a bronze medal (3rd place) in the junior foil individual bracket. Gomes is currently ranked No. 49 in the world’s junior category after taking bronze at the Junior Pan American Championship. She’s currently No. 100 globally in the senior category and has the Photo courtesy of cbesgrima.org.br Rafaella Gomes stands proudly with her bronze medal at the 2021 Junior Pan American Championship. third-highest senior ranking for the Brazil National Team. As a freshman at UC San Diego, Gomes reached the NCAA National Championship on March 27 and qualified for the prestigious tournament after taking silver at the NCAA West Regional Championship out of 11 competitors on March 12. She also finished second in the Mountain Pacific Sports Federation Fencing Championships’ Women’s Foil on March 13, earning her the MPSF Newcomer of the Year award. Gomes is now training for the 2022 Senior World Championships in Cairo, Egypt, which takes place July 15-23. She is working with the Massialas Foundation in San Francisco and U.S. Men’s Foil Fencing Team’s coach Greg Massialas, which has churned out Olympic talent over the years. Below is her training regimen ahead of the World Championships. What is your workout program this summer? Fencing goes year-round. When I am not competing for UC San Diego in the NCAA circuit, I am competing in the Brazilian national circuit. Because I do not have an off season, my training program changes all the time at the mercy of my competition schedule. No matter where I am though, I stretch every morning and night, and I run every morning I am able. If I have access to a gym, I follow the training program I learned from UC San Diego coach Patrick McLeroy, who works with the entire UCSD fencing team. What are your fitness goals for this summer? First, recovery. I am working to get back to where I was athletically before I caught COVID19. Once there, I will be focusing on increasing my explosive strength and decreasing my reaction time. How are you measuring your development? I am measuring my development by comparing it to where I was before I caught COVID. Quantitatively, I can compare how heavy I lift or how fast I run now as opposed to then. I can compare how easily I tire or how effectively I execute technical skills. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I have practice at the Massialas Foundation every week day and Saturdays for two hours. Practice includes 30 minutes of intense, fencing-specific footwork drills, an hour of fencing, and 30 minutes of one-on-one work with a coach. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? I ended my first season in the Brazilian national circuit as a new member of the Brazilian national junior and senior teams. My results include two silver and two bronze medals, one of each for the junior and senior categories. No athlete can foresee every roadblock to their goals or the outcome of every competition, so focus on what you can control. Focus on the process, and be consistent. articles.text: 1,800-year old Methuselah Tree & prehistoric Tafoni Rock Formation El Corte de Madera Creek Preserve in San Mateo County has some easily accessible features that many more acclaimed destinations in the Bay Area don’t come close to offering. Located near Highway 35 (Skyline Boulevard) is a tree that predates the Europeans settling of America, the estimated 1,800-year old Methuselah Tree. It is the only old growth redwood tree in the Santa Cruz Mountains outside of Big Basin State Park and is known as the “Big Old Tree on Skyline.” The Peninsula Open Space Preserve describes the Methuselah Tree as having sprouted in 217 AD, experiencing Ohlone natives bark cultivation in 1,000 AD, and witnessing European settlers and Mexico’s independence from Spain in 1821. Lumber mills in the 1870s’ California Gold Rush likely determined that its massive burl made Methuselah impossible to harvest. In our visit in December 2020, the entrance to the tree was closed due to dry conditions, but it has since re-opened to the public. It’s an excellent place for a photo-op and starting point for a day of hiking. You can walk up to the Big Old Tree and sit on its stump. Across from the Methuselah Tree is the Sierra Morena Trail, the starting point for a 1.5 mile hike to another historic landmark—the Tafoni Rock Formation. The nearly 40-foot tall hunk of sandstone is an estimated 30 million years old. A platform sits at its base with informative panels and a close view. The rock formation, Tafoni, is a name that describes the sandstone’s cavernous result of weathering. coast, as wind and waves eat away at shorelines. El Corte de Madera’s represents a prehistoric time, dating back to the middle of the Cenozoic Era when the ocean covered San Mateo County. A half-mile away from the rock formation, continuing on the Fir Trail, is Vista Point, another place of note. The overlook has a narrow view of the Pacific Ocean and a bench for resting and viewing. An interesting memorial to an air wreckage in the 1950s sits at the point’s entrance. It was erected in 2006 to commemorate a British Commonwealth Pacific Airlines commercial airplane that was bound for Sydney, Australia, but crashed during a storm in October 1953. One can still find pieces of the wreckage on the park’s Resolution Trail. From there, continuing back to the car rounds out your day at a mellow 3.6 miles. But continuing past the Tafoni Rock formation on the Tafoni Trail – turning right when exiting the pathway from the giant chunk of stone – will provide a 5.15 mile day and slightly under 1,000 feet in elevation gain—while surrounding you with redwood trees and stumps from old giants. When considering that 49 of the hikers we saw were in the first 2.1 miles from the trailhead to Vista Point and the Tafoni formation, this loop is certainly in the “hidden treasure” category. The trails are a common place for mountain bikers zooming downhill and off berms, meaning no dogs are allowed in El Corte de Madera Creek. articles.text: You may have noticed an alert on your phone or email this week about king tides impacting the Bay Area. It is an event that results in higher tides typically in evening hours, which is expected to cause flooding in several lowland locations in the coming days. The predicted king tides are expected to last longer than usual and could continue this week through Friday, July 15. This natural phenomenon typically occurs during the winter months when the sun and moon reach their closest points to Earth. However, king tides return around the summer solstice two weeks ago. “King Tides happen around the solstices, when the alignment of the sun, moon, and Earth creates a stronger pull on the tides, resulting in higher high tides and lower low tides,” said Annie Kohut Frankel of the California Coastal Commission. The National Weather Services announced it expected the first high tide to arrive in San Francisco last night, Tuesday, July 12, with tides of up to 7-1/2 feet near the Embarcadero around midnight. On Thursday, July 14, a tide of 7.51 feet is expected. Flooding in Sausalito occurred on Monday, July 11 with the northbound Highway 101 offramp to Stinson Beach closed. Mill Valley’s Tamalpais junction is susceptible to flooding. articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA)’s exhibition celebrating Edith Heath, designer and founder of Heath Ceramics, is on display now through October 30. Edith Heath: A Life in Clay showcases the legacy of the artist who founded Heath Ceramics. The exhibit includes over 50 pieces of ceramics, clay samples, photographs, and personal memorabilia on display. A documentary video is shown inside the museum as well. The new exhibition introduces visitors to the artist’s career, which was deeply expressive of California’s land and lifestyle. Heath, who died in 2005, focused on creating dependable and long-lasting products for the home, with a focus on sustainability. A Life in Clay was organized by OMCA Curator of Photography Drew Johnson, and guest curator Jennifer Volland. “Edith Heath transformed our notion of ‘good design’ pioneering a new aesthetic of natural, stylish yet functional products made from local materials and designed to endure,” said Johnson. “As an icon of quintessential California design who lived and worked in Sausalito and San Francisco, OMCA is excited to share the extraordinary story of Heath’s life and legacy.” A Life in Clay examines Heath’s technical experimentations with native California clays and glaze formulas. Her love of natural landscapes shaped the quality of her design and inspired her to seek clays from California rather than what was traditionally used for dinnerware. “What began as a rebellion against imported white clay more than 50 years ago is now a modern-day classic,” said Volland, who has researched the artist since 2014 and served as an essayist for the book Edith Heath: Philosophies. To learn more about the exhibition, and to purchase tickets, visit www.museumca.org. Photo by Christina Cueto The newest collection at Oakland Museum of California showcases Edith Heath’s ceramics.
articles.title: Edith Heath exhibit continues through October at Oakland Museum

articles.text: The Fifth Annual Piedmont Chamber Music Festival, the only weeklong residency chamber music festival in the East Bay, celebrates returning to live concerts this summer with three public performances at the Piedmont Center for the Arts opening on Wednesday, July 20. Festival musicians will explore the theme “Human. Alone and Together” in works from composers old and new that remind one that life is better together. Led by founders Wayne Lee (violin) a Piedmont native, and his wife Juliana Han (piano), the festival features eight internationally acclaimed musicians from throughout the U.S. Returning musicians Jasmine Lin (violin) and Deborah Pae (cello), will be joined by guest musicians Teng Li (Principal Violinist, Los Angeles Philharmonic), Francisco Fullana (violin), Paul Laraia (viola), and Clancy Newman (cellist & composer), back by popular demand. This Week’s Featured Artists: WAYNE LEE, Piano, JULIANA HAN, Piano American violinist Wayne Lee has enjoyed a prolific career worldwide as a member of two internationally-acclaimed chamber ensembles. Since 2012, he has been a member of the Formosa Quartet, a string quartet that performs extensively in North America, Europe and Asia, with recent engagements at London’s Wigmore Hall, the Berlin Philharmonie, Taipei’s National Concert Hall, and the Chan Centre for the Performing Arts in Vancouver. For over a decade he was a member of the Manhattan Piano Trio, an ensemble acclaimed as “outstanding” by the Washington Post and lauded as “a grand departure from the usual” by the News Herald. A dedicated teacher and arts advocate, Wayne has previously taught at the University of Illinois at Champaign-Urbana and the Juilliard School in New York. Pianist Juliana Han is an active collaborator, chamber musician, and soloist, lauded not only for her inspired performances but also for her musical lectures, which illuminate classical works for diverse audiences. She has performed in notable venues across North America and Asia, including Carnegie Hall, Alice Tully Hall, and the National Taichung Theater. Her other festival appearances include Music Academy of the West, Norfolk Chamber Music Festival, and Kneisel Hall Chamber Music Festival. Violinist Wayne Lee and pianist Juliana Han will lead the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival next week in its fifth summer at the Piedmont Center for the Arts.

articles.text: Django Reinhardt was born January 23, 1910 in Liberchies, Pont-à-Celles, Belgium into a family of Manouche Romani descent. Romani is an IndoAryan ethnic group that originated in Northern India (Rajasthan and Punjab). Manouche is the French group of Romani people. His legal name-was Jean Reinhardt, but he was known as “Django”, a Gypsy name meaning “I awake.” Django married at 17. A year later, he accidentally knocked over a candle in the wagon he shared with his wife and started a fire with the celluloid his wife used for making artificial flowers. They escaped the fire, but over half of Django’s body was burned. He was told he would never play guitar again. Though he only had full use of his fretting hand index and middle fingers (his ring and little fingers could only fret chords), he went on to become one of the greatest jazz guitarists of all time! I know what that’s like. When I was 22, I cut my fretting hand middle finger to the bone with a circular saw and the surgeon said I would never play guitar again. Unacceptable! I worked hard for six months and recovered. Twenty years later, the finger recovered nerve sensation. Django and violinist Stéphane Grappelli separately made a living in the 1920’s busking (playing for donations) on the streets of Paris. In 1928, Grappelli was a member of the orchestra at the Ambassador Hotel while bandleader Paul Whiteman and jazz violinist Joe Venuti were performing there. Grappelli modeled his playing after Venuti. From 1934-1939, Django and Grappelli played together in the Quintette du Hot Club de France, originally Legendary “gypsy guitarist” Django Reinhardt. at the club in the Hotel Claridge, but the Quintette name was used in performances across Europe. Django was an “ear player”, building his phrases from a creative aural perspective in the vocal context (thinking like an improvising vocalist). In transcribing his solos, I suspected he was listening to his imagination, rather than his logical-mathematical left brain. Charlie Christian played with the same perspective, based on “feel” and modeled much of his style after Django. Topsy, the example of Django’s improvisational style linked below, is based on the Andalusian cadence, a middle-eastern chord progression brought into Spain during the Arabic civilization in Spain (1711-1492). In the key of C minor, the Andalusian cadence is Cm-Bb-Ab-G. The second chord in the main progression of Topsy, C minor with Bb bass, functions much like Bb major. The Ab7 darkens the key, including the “Gb” note (the dark flat five of C minor). Starring Review by Chris Honoré If you’re a fan of the adrenaline-producing, jump ball, game clock is ticking, pedal-to-themetal, flat out thriller, well, don’t miss Taken. It’s an unpretentious rush. Forget any minor plot holes. Just sit back and enjoy. It was co-written by Luc Beeson (Transporter series and Tell No One), whose films define slickness and are meant to be visceral rather than cerebral. The cinematography and the script in Taken conspire to create a sense of motion that accelerates until act III gives the audience whiplash. It’s always a pleasure to watch Liam Neeson, no matter the role. He’s a fine, versatile actor. In Taken he portrays Bryan Mills, a retired black ops CIA agent who has left the agency to be closer to his 17-year-old daughter, Kim (Maggie Grace), who lives with her mother (Famke Janssen) and very rich stepfather (Xander Berkeley) in Los Angeles. The setup of the film is straightforward while steeped in foreboding. Kim begs her mother and father to let her go to Paris for the summer with her best girlfriend. They’re going to live in a swank penthouse of some friends and tour the City of Lights. Bryan is not pleased, knowing that there are dangers in the world that his ex-wife and daughter are simply unaware of. Finally, he relents and gives Kim an international phone while insisting she call him twice daily. Within one hour of landing in Paris and arriving at the apartment, the girls are kidnapped. And so begins a classic hunt film, predictable to be sure, but also entertaining. Bryan is lethal and refuses to collaborate with the French police. Alone, he searches for what turns out to be a ruthless ring of Albanian white slavers that auction off women to international buyers like sports cars. He has 96 hours, he’s told, to find Kim and her friend before they are sold and swept away into a brutal world from which they will never return. What happens next, well, if you’re a fan of the kidnap genre, Liam Neeson stars in Taken. nothing will surprise. But this isn’t a film about surprises; rather, it’s a hard case revenge/ vigilante tale that appeals to all of our baser instincts – in a good way. It features one very angry father willing to do whatever it takes to find his daughter. And who wouldn’t? It helps, of course, if you happen to be a highly trained covert agent with some very cool skill sets. Let the games begin. Taken. Directed by Pierre Morel. Starring Liam Neeson, Famke Janssen and Maggie Grace. 1 hr., 31 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2009. Now streaming on Prime/Apple tv. A scene from Taken.

Review by Chris Honoré Helen Mirren and Christopher Plummer were both nominated for Oscars for their portrayals of Sofya and Leo Tolstoy in The Last Station, released in 2009. No doubt, they are two of the most accomplished actors working today, their talent astonishing. They clearly relish their roles as the aging Tolstoys who were partners for over 40 years as Leo wrote massive books such as Anna Karenina and War and Peace. articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s Ratatouille. As a work of animation and imaginative story telling, Ratatouille is extraordinary. At its center is Remy (Patton Oswalt), a Parisian rat who along with his large family plies the suburban garbage cans for food that he considers simply awful. And because of his reluctance to consume what they can scavenge, he is told repeatedly by his father, Django (Brian Dennehey), head of the clan, to “eat his garbage!” But when the family is forced to leave their cottage home (they live in the ceiling), Remy is separated from everyone and is swept away into a storm drain. He ends up in front of a famous restaurant named after its celebrity chef, Gusteau (Brad Garret). It’s there that Remy begins to hang around the kitchen and meets up with the restaurant’s dishwasher, Alfredo Linguini (Lou Romero). Remy, who has a refined palate and a nose to match, plus a dream to become a chef, convinces his new-found friend to be his front man, allowing Remy to burrow into in Linguini’s hair, and, with tugs and pulls, gives his new partner (who has not a shred of cooking ability) directions. Initially, the pair save an awful soup using Remy’s special seasoning. In other words, Remy becomes the master puppeteer. Meanwhile, the effete food critic, Anton Ego (Peter O’Toole), visits the restaurant and gives his meal an awful critique, so bad that it breaks Gusteau’s heart, allowing a greedy, self-serving sous-chef named Skinner (Ian Holm), to take the master chef’s place. Soon, however, the restaurant is in trouble, its reputation falling into disrepute, the meals poorly prepared by Skinner. But Remy and Linguini come to the rescue, along with the help of Collette Tatou (Janeane Garofalo), and create some astonishingly wonderful dishes, while Remy reaches new heights in preparing French cuisine. The two also anticipate the return of Anton Ego. But there is a crisis, and Remy calls in his clan for help. They go through the kitchen dishwasher to get clean, and then assist Remy/ Linguini in getting a superb meal together, acting as the creators of delicious sauces. Not surprisingly, Anton Ego does return, only this time gives the restaurant a glowing review. Indeed, the story gets a bit complicated by the discovery that Linguini is actually Gusteau’s abandoned son, which brings up the question of who actually owns the restaurant. Ratatouille is a remarkable demonstration of the genius of Pixar Studios: its colors and textures are truly outstanding, and the story one that will delight the entire family, not just the little guys. It’s an animated feature not to be missed. Ratatouille. Directed by Brad Bird. Pixar animation. With the voices of Patton Oswalt, Ian Holm, Lou Romano. 1 hr., 51 min. Rated G. Released to theaters in the 2007. Now streaming on Wudu/Prime/Disney+.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Released in 1993, Free Willy is a family-friendly drama that will undoubtedly appeal to a new generation of kids. At the center of this most engaging film are a 7,000-pound Orca whale named Willy, and a 12-year-old boy, Jessie (Jason James Richter), who are both struggling to adjust to their situations. For Willy, captured while swimming with his pod (think family), it’s the confines of the Northwest Adventure theme park. Jesse, an orphan who was abandoned by his mother at a very early age, grew up in various foster homes, but prefers to hustle on the streets with his urchin buds, scrounging for spare change, and begging for food from the back door of local restaurants. Both Willy and Jesse have an attitude. Willy refuses to work with his trainer, Rae (Lori Petty), and Jesse is surly and filled with resentment at life in general. It’s obvious that if something doesn’t happen to turn Jesse around, he will slip through the cracks and be lost for good. One night, Jesse sneaks into a theme park with a can of spray paint, intent on leaving behind his signature graffiti. He begins with a window overlooking one of the large water tanks where the Orcas perform. He is interrupted by the police who give him three mandatory options: return the next day and clean the window, move in with a foster family, Glen and Annie Greenwood (Jane Atkinson and Michel Madsen), who have agreed to give him a home, or take a hard pass and go to juvi. Not eager to go to jail, Jesse agrees to live with the Greenwoods, and returns to the park to scrub the observation window. Walking by the tank, Jesse is warned by Rae to be careful, there’s an Orca just below the surface. Ignoring Rae, of course, he slips and falls in. But to the surprise of Rae and other park employees, to include the owners of Northwest, Willy gently lifts Jesse out of the water and places him gently onto the side of the pool. Now living with the Greenwoods, Jesse sneaks out at night, and returns to the tank and sits on the side, playing his harmonica. Willy hears him and swims over. And so the two begin to bond. By Chris Honoré As a work of animation and imaginative story telling, Ratatouille is extraordinary. At its center is Remy (Patton Oswalt), a Parisian rat who along with his large family plies the suburban garbage cans for food that he considers simply awful. And because of his reluctance to consume what they can scavenge, he is told repeatedly by his father, Django (Brian Dennehey), head of the clan, to “eat his garbage!” But when the family is forced to leave their cottage home (they live in the ceiling), Remy is separated from everyone and is swept away into a storm drain. He ends up in front of a famous restaurant named after its celebrity chef, Gusteau (Brad Garret). It’s there that Remy begins to hang around the kitchen and meets up with the restaurant’s dishwasher, Alfredo Linguini (Lou Romero). Remy, who has a refined palate and a nose to match, plus a dream to become a chef, convinces his new-found friend to be his front man, allowing Remy to burrow into in Linguini’s hair, and, with tugs and pulls, gives his new partner (who has not a shred of cooking ability) directions. Initially, the pair save an awful soup using Remy’s special seasoning. In other words, Remy becomes the master puppeteer. Meanwhile, the effete food critic, Anton Ego (Peter O’Toole), visits the restaurant and gives his meal an awful critique, so bad that it breaks Gusteau’s heart, allowing a greedy, self-serving sous-chef named Skinner (Ian Holm), to take the master chef’s place. Soon, however, the restaurant is in trouble, its reputation falling into disrepute, the meals poorly prepared by Skinner. But Remy and Linguini come to the rescue, along with the help of Collette Tatou (Janeane Garofalo), and create some astonishingly wonderful dishes, while Remy reaches new heights in preparing French cuisine. The two also anticipate the return of Anton Ego. But there is a crisis, and Remy calls in his clan for help. They go through the kitchen dishwasher to get clean, and then assist Remy/ Linguini in getting a superb meal together, acting as the creators of delicious sauces. Not surprisingly, Anton Ego does return, only this time gives the restaurant a glowing review. Indeed, the story gets a bit complicated by the discovery that Linguini is actually Gusteau’s abandoned son, which brings up the question of who actually owns the restaurant. Ratatouille is a remarkable demonstration of the genius of Pixar Studios: its colors and textures are truly outstanding, and the story one that will delight the entire family, not just the little guys. It’s an animated feature not to be missed. Ratatouille. Directed by Brad Bird. Pixar animation. With the voices of Patton Oswalt, Ian Holm, Lou Romano. 1 hr., 51 min. Rated G. articles.text: Frank Anderson, a life-long Piedmont resident and a former Piedmont Vice Mayor, passed away peacefully at his longtime home in Piedmont on May 24, 2022. Born Frank Stoakes Anderson in Oakland in 1928, he was the son of David L. Anderson and Marguerite Stoakes Anderson. He started as a kindergartener at Havens Elementary School and graduated from Piedmont High School in 1946. He regaled his family with stories of working at Buzz’s gas station in Piedmont and his time as a yell-leader for PHS. He graduated from University of California Berkeley in 1950 with a Bachelor’s degree in Business Administration, followed by Army service at Fort Leonard Wood, Mo. Frank went to work for Fred J. Early Construction Company in San Francisco as a project manager and estimator. He then launched his own company, Anderson Constructors, Inc., which had offices in San Francisco and Oakland, specializing in commercial tenant improvements and insurance restoration work. Through his work, Frank got to know many great restauranteurs in San Francisco and was a member of the city’s Merchants Exchange Club. Frank was dedicated to Piedmont and for a stint was the city’s Vice Mayor. Frank Anderson, a lifelong Piedmont resident and former Vice Mayor, died on May 24. He was 94. Frank skied throughout Europe and was a season ticket holder at Squaw Valley in California for more than 40 years. He enjoyed many sailing adventures with his friends, loved biking with the Piedmont Pedal Pushers, and was an avid duck and upland game bird hunter. Frank is predeceased by his wife Lill, who passed the same day in 2016. He is survived by his brother David; his children Jeff, Richard, Kelly, Fredrik and Kristen, and his six grandchildren Michael and Tyler, Ben and Evan, and Andreas and Markus. A true bon vivant, Frank will be missed by many, near and far. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests a memorial donation be made to the Piedmont Beautification Foundation or Planned Parenthood.

The Walking on Wednesdays group had another great day for walking on July 6 and had a strong turnout of 32 walkers and two K-9 best friends. The group was pleased to welcome back 8-year-old Charles Katzel and father Aaron for a second summer walk. It also welcomed first-time walkers Martha Swartz and Meghan Bennett with them. Meghan grew up in Piedmont, and has created the “History of Piedmont” website (https://www. historyofpiedmont.com) with information that the group has used on its walks. Two weeks earlier the walkers had gone to Piedmont streets that were on the early 20th Century Key System streetcar Numbers 10 and 12 lines. The 10 line went from Piedmont Avenue in Oakland to Crocker Park, and the 12 line went down Fairview Avenue to Grand Avenue and downtown Oakland. There were two other Key System lines in Piedmont, and the walkers thought it would be good to complete their Key System exploration with a walk to where the C and 11 lines also once ran. A quick Key System refresher was provided. In the 1890s land developer Frank C. Havens and his partner Francis Marion “Borax” Smith established “The Realty Syndicate” that acquired large tracts of undeveloped land throughout the East Bay for homes. The Key System was conceived by Smith as a way to sell the syndicate’s land. The Key System began service in 1903 in Berkeley and in 1904 in what was to become the City of Piedmont. On her website Bennett provides lots of information on Piedmont and the Key System. She reports that shortly after Piedmont was incorporated in 1907, the B electric car line from Trestle Glen and the C line from 41st Street and Piedmont Avenue, provided connections to the ferry terminal in West Oakland. In 1924, the C line was extended to its terminus at Oakland Avenue and Latham Street in Piedmont. Following completion of the Bay Bridge, the Key System provided direct rail service on both lines to San Francisco. The No. 11 Oakland Avenue line ran from Rio Vista Avenue near the Kaiser Hospital up Piedmont Avenue to Linda Avenue, and then down Oakland Avenue and Broadway to 7th Street. The line was started as a part of Consolidated Piedmont Cable in 1892 and was later electrified. As a cable line, this route ascended the steep Oakland Avenue hill using a long gravity loop. This was not practical as an electric line, so the route was divided with the steep hill line abandoned, and the lower end diverted via a private rightof-way to Piedmont and Linda Avenues, thus avoiding the heavy grades. At the about time the Bay Bridge was opening in 1936, National City Lines, a small bus fleet in Minnesota, was organized into a holding company with equity funding from General Motors, Firestone Rubber, Phillips Petroleum, Standard Oil of California, and Mack Trucks. It began purchasing local transportation systems across the United States. It was a corporate conspiracy to monopolize the sale of buses across the United States, The buses were made by Mack and GM, that were exclusively fueled by Phillips and Standard gasoline, and driven on Firestone tires. By 1946, it controlled 46 transportation companies in 45 cities across 16 states. National City Lines tore up the tracks and the overhead wires and burned the trolley and train cars. In 1946, it acquired a majority stake of Key System stock and slowly began dismantling the system. The local streetcar lines were replaced by buses after World War II, with the right-of-ways converted to other uses, including parks and private homes. On June 26, 1948, the Key System rail service on Oakland Avenue was replaced by buses. The Transbay trains to Piedmont stopped running and the Key System was dismantled in 1958. In 1960, the Key System was sold to the newly formed public agency, AC Transit. In 1949, a Federal Court convicted National City Lines, General Motors, Standard Oil of California, Firestone Tire, and others of criminally conspiring to monopolize the sale of buses and related products to their subsidiary transit companies throughout the U.S. and violating the Sherman Anti-Trust Act. However, they were only fined $5,000. Some corporate executives were found criminally guilty, but only fined $1. With all this Key System information and understanding from Meghan Bennett’s History of Piedmont website, the group was ready to walk. They started off going up Highland Avenue to Oakland Avenue which was part of the Number 10 line. The walkers turned down Oakland to Latham Street, the only Piedmont roadway named “street.” This was where the C line ended. Some of the houses that were built along Latham were noted for their long, narrow footprints that allowed them to fit on the strip of Key System right-of-way land after the trains stopped running. The walkers turned on Blair Avenue and went up York Drive. At Holly Place it was noted that this was once a stop on the C line, and that a pathway in the middle of the block on York goes up to Ricardo Avenue. This made it easier for riders to get to the trains. Charlene Louie shared old photos of the trains with still recognizable homes in the background. The group came to Arroyo Avenue, where the C line merged with the 10 line, and went down Pleasant Valley Avenue to Piedmont Avenue. The walkers went up Arroyo, crossed Pleasant Valley, and started up Rose Avenue. Rose is on the Piedmont/Oakland border with homes on its north side in Oakland and on the south side in Piedmont. articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWV) will discuss Laboratories of Autocracy: A Wake-Up Call from Behind the Lines by David Pepper at its upcoming book meeting on August 16. Pepper’s Laboratories shows the “high profile antics of national politics,” and spotlights what can often be corruption in statehouses across the nation, which the author asserts pose the greatest threat to American democracy. The book outlines 30 steps that need to be taken, from federal action to individual steps, to help fight corruption in their own communities. Pepper is a writer, lawyer, former elected official, and served as the Chairman of the Ohio Democratic Party between 2015 and 2021. He earned his B.A. from Yale University and his J.D. from Yale Law School. Havens and his partner Francis Marion “Borax” Smith established “The Realty Syndicate” that acquired large tracts of undeveloped land throughout the East Bay for homes. The Key System was conceived by Smith as a way to sell the syndicate’s land. The Key System began service in 1903 in Berkeley and in 1904 in what was to become the City of Piedmont. On her website Bennett provides lots of information on Piedmont and the Key System. She reports that shortly after Piedmont was incorporated in 1907, the B electric car line from Trestle Glen and the C line from 41st Street and Piedmont Avenue, provided connections to the ferry terminal in West Oakland. In 1924, the C line was extended to its terminus at Oakland Avenue and Latham Street in Piedmont. Following completion of the Bay Bridge, the Key System provided direct rail service on both lines to San Francisco. The No. 11 Oakland Avenue line ran from Rio Vista Avenue near the Kaiser Hospital up Piedmont Avenue to Linda Avenue, and then down Oakland Avenue and Broadway to 7th Street. The line was started as a part of Consolidated Piedmont Cable in 1892 and was later electrified. As a cable line, this route ascended the steep Oakland Avenue hill using a long gravity loop. This was not practical as an electric line, so the route was divided with the steep hill line abandoned, and the lower end diverted via a private rightof-way to Piedmont and Linda Avenues, thus avoiding the heavy grades. At the about time the Bay Bridge was opening in 1936, National City Lines, a small bus fleet in Minnesota, was organized into a holding company with equity funding from General Motors, Firestone Rubber, Phillips Petroleum, Standard Oil of California, and Mack Trucks. It began purchasing local transportation systems across the United States. It was a corporate conspiracy to monopolize the sale of buses across the United States, The buses were made by Mack and GM, that were exclusively fueled by Phillips and Standard gasoline, and driven on Firestone tires. By 1946, it controlled 46 transportation companies in 45 cities across 16 states. National City Lines tore up the tracks and the overhead wires and burned the trolley and train cars. In 1946, it acquired a majority stake of Key System stock and slowly began dismantling the system. The local streetcar lines were replaced by buses after World War II, with the right-of-ways converted to other uses, including parks and private homes. On June 26, 1948, the Key System rail service on Oakland Avenue was replaced by buses. The Transbay trains to Piedmont stopped running and the Key System was dismantled in 1958. In 1960, the Key System was sold to the newly formed public agency, AC Transit. In 1949, a Federal Court convicted National City Lines, General Motors, Standard Oil of California, Firestone Tire, and others of criminally conspiring to monopolize the sale of buses and related products to their subsidiary transit companies throughout the U.S. and violating the Sherman Anti-Trust Act. However, they were only fined $5,000. Some corporate executives were found criminally guilty, but only fined $1. With all this Key System information and understanding from Meghan Bennett’s History of Piedmont website, the group was ready to walk. They started off going up Highland Avenue to Oakland Avenue which was part of the Number 10 line. The walkers turned down Oakland to Latham Street, the only Piedmont roadway named “street.” This was where the C line ended. Some of the houses that were built along Latham were noted for their long, narrow footprints that allowed them to fit on the strip of Key System right-of-way land after the trains stopped running. The walkers turned on Blair Avenue and went up York Drive. At Holly Place it was noted that this was once a stop on the C line, and that a pathway in the middle of the block on York goes up to Ricardo Avenue. This made it easier for riders to get to the trains. Charlene Louie shared old photos of the trains with still recognizable homes in the background. The group came to Arroyo Avenue, where the C line merged with the 10 line, and went down Pleasant Valley Avenue to Piedmont Avenue. The walkers went up Arroyo, crossed Pleasant Valley, and started up Rose Avenue. Rose is on the Piedmont/Oakland border with homes on its north side in Oakland and on the south side in Piedmont. articles.text: Every home remodeling project is driven by budget and schedule. A reputable General Contractor will give you a detailed written scope of both. No doubt, you expect your contractor to stick to the deal. Every project will have surprises, what we call “unforeseen circumstances”. An old pipe in a wall, dry rot around a window, electrical wiring not up to code. These types of issues will increase the cost of your project, typically done by a written change order. More than two years into the pandemic, most of us have experienced some frustration with global supply chain issues. As remodelers, we are not immune. Some kitchen appliances have a 12-month lead time. Bathroom fixtures – even a simple towel bar - can take six months to arrive. Recessed lights are delayed by months because of computer chip shortages. Window production lead times can exceed six months. Orders of locally made tile, which relies on raw materials from abroad, are outstanding for up to eight months. Promised delivery dates are not being met. Does this impact your project’s budget and schedule? Yes! Using the example of tile, for a bathroom, if the product doesn’t arrive on time, a domino effect of delays occurs. Cabinetry, countertops, plumbing, electrical/lighting, finish carpentry and painting can all be pushed out. Add to this the overall high demand for qualified contractors and you have a scheduling disaster. No surprise – in remodeling, time equals money. So, what can you do? The first thing is, select a General Contractor who communicates with you from the beginning on potential issues. Be prepared that with any project delay you are likely to incur additional costs for materials, shipping and labor. Some homeowners expect their remodeler to pay for these extras since they contracted at a fixed price. With the small profit margins in construction, contractors are simply unable to absorb the additional costs. Even for the most experienced remodeler, the past couple of years have been a painful education. The good news is we have learned to not delay in decision-making. We order desired items immediately – even without a fully designed project. Homeowners are putting aside extra funds for unanticipated costs. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, July 13, 2022 RELYING ON EXPERIENCE Every home remodeling project is driven by budget and schedule. A reputable General Contractor will give you a detailed written scope of both. No doubt, you expect your contractor to stick to the deal. Every project will have surprises, what we call “unforeseen circumstances”. An old pipe in a wall, dry rot around a window, electrical wiring not up to code. These types of issues will increase the cost of your project, typically done by a written change order. More than two years into the pandemic, most of us have experienced some frustration with global supply chain issues. As remodelers, we are not immune. Some kitchen appliances have a 12-month lead time. Bathroom fixtures – even a simple towel bar - can take six months to arrive. Recessed lights are delayed by months because of computer chip shortages. Window production lead times can exceed six months. Orders of locally made tile, which relies on raw materials from abroad, are outstanding for up to eight months. Promised delivery dates are Remodeling delays: whose fault is it? not being met. Does this impact your project’s budget and schedule? Yes! Using the example of tile, for a bathroom, if the product doesn’t arrive on time, a domino effect of delays occurs. Cabinetry, countertops, plumbing, electrical/lighting, finish carpentry and painting can all be pushed out. Add to this the overall high demand for qualified contractors and you have a scheduling disaster. No surprise – in remodeling, time equals money. So, what can you do? The first thing is, select a General Contractor who communicates with you from the beginning on potential issues. Be prepared that with any project delay you are likely to incur additional costs for materials, shipping and labor. Some homeowners expect their remodeler to pay for these extras since they contracted at a fixed price. With the small profit margins in construction, contractors are simply unable to absorb the additional costs. Even for the most experienced remodeler, the past couple of years have been a painful education. The good news is we have learned to not delay in decision-making. We order desired items immediately – even without a fully designed project. Homeowners are putting aside extra funds for unanticipated costs. The keys to maintaining a good contractor-client relationship are communication, transparency, patience and kindness. articles.text: NASA describes this photo as follows: “What looks much like craggy mountains on a moonlit evening is actually the edge of a nearby, young, star-forming region NGC 3324 in the Carina Nebula.” NASA released the first high resolution photographs from the James Webb Space Telescope, on July 11. This striking image of star birth dubbed “‘Cosmic Cliffs” is 7,600 light years away and shows the edge of a gigantic, gaseous cavity in the Carina Nebula. The Webb telescope is a joint partnership of NASA, the European Space Agency and Canadian Space Agency. President Biden was given the honor of unveiling the first of the greatly awaited images on Monday, and four more were released yesterday. The James Webb telescope uses infrared light by the Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam). NIRCam was built by a team at the University of Arizona and Lockheed Martin’s Advanced Technology Center. This image reveals previously obscured areas of star birth. The cavernous area has been carved from the nebula by the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from extremely massive, hot, young stars located in the center of the bubble, not seen, but above the image. The high-energy radiation from these stars sculps the nebula’s wall by slowly eroding it away. NIRCam – with its crisp resolution and unparalleled sensitivity – unveils hundreds of previously hidden stars, and even numerous background galaxies. NASA explains the features in the image. The “steam” that appears to rise from the celestial “mountains” is actually hot, ionized gas and hot dust streaming away from the nebula due to intense, ultraviolet radiation. Dramatic pillars rise above the glowing wall of gas, resisting the blistering ultraviolet radiation from the young stars. Bubbles and cavities are being blown by the intense radiation and stellar winds of newborn stars. Protostellar jets and outflows, which appear in gold, shoot from dust-enshrouded, nascent stars. A “blow-out” erupts at the top-center of the ridge, spewing gas and dust into the interstellar medium. An unusual “arch” appears, looking like a bent-over cylinder. This period of very early star formation is difficult to capture since it lasts only about 50,000 to 100,000 years. The full set of the telescope’s first full-color images and spectroscopic data, which uncover a collection of cosmic features elusive until now, were released on July 12 and are available nu NASA at: Nasa.gov/webbfirstimages.
